record.original_question: Must every graph with exactly three distinct adjacency eigenvalues have at most three distinct vertex degrees?

evidence.quote: Problem 3.6. Does a graph with three distinct eigenvalues have at most three distinct degrees?

artifact.self_contained_problem: Let $G$ be a finite simple graph with adjacency matrix $A(G)$, and let the spectrum of $G$ be the multiset of eigenvalues of $A(G)$. Suppose that $A(G)$ has exactly three distinct eigenvalues. Must the number of distinct vertex degrees of $G$ be at most three?
artifact.status_search_result: This is a well-known open question, often attributed to de Caen. Connected graphs with four or five distinct adjacency eigenvalues can have arbitrarily many distinct vertex degrees (constructions by van Dam and collaborators), but no example is known of a graph with three distinct eigenvalues having more than three distinct degrees, and the question remains unresolved in recent surveys and research articles on graphs with three distinct eigenvalues.

status_evidence.title: The coherent rank of a graph with three eigenvalues
status_evidence.snippet: A question by De Caen remains open regarding graphs with three distinct eigenvalues; the condition of three eigenvalues is critical, since there exist connected graphs with four or five distinct eigenvalues and arbitrarily many valencies.
status_evidence.claim: The de Caen-type question on whether three distinct eigenvalues forces at most three distinct degrees is still open.

status_evidence.title: Graphs with many valencies and few eigenvalues
status_evidence.snippet: Constructions of connected graphs with four or five distinct eigenvalues and arbitrarily many distinct valencies.
status_evidence.claim: For four or more distinct eigenvalues, the analogous degree-bound fails, but the three-eigenvalue case is left open.
